description: Somos un equipo enfocado en llevar la exploración espacial al siguiente nivel educativo mediante Realidad Virtual e interacción inmersiva con Meta Quest. Para el desafío 'Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer', estamos desarrollando un juego interactivo en VR donde los estudiantes asumen el rol de comandantes de una base en marte
summary: We developed Marsianics, a browser-based WebXR simulator built with Three.js that runs seamlessly on both VR headsets (like the Meta Quest 3) and standard laptops—requiring no downloads or expensive hardware. Designed to bridge the STEM career gap for high school students in underserved communities, the game puts players in charge of the first human base on Mars. Using real scientific data from NASA, the JPL, and the Canadian Space Agency—including radiation levels, space weather, and Earth-to-Mars communication delays—students must manage oxygen, water, food, energy, and communications to survive seven days. Through hands-on problem-solving, they explore real space-industry careers in robotics, hydroponics, telecommunications, and life support, empowering them to envision a future in STEM regardless of their economic background
details:
Marsianics: project description

What it does and how it works

Marsianics is a virtual reality survival and management game set in an underground outpost built by the first humans on Mars. You play the station’s operator, not an action hero. Your job is to keep the base and its crew alive for 7 accelerated Martian days, which takes about 42 minutes in real time.

The base has six rooms arranged in a star around a central hub:

  • Control room: the main computer, time controls, a crew health monitor and a rover console.
  • Telecom: a dish antenna you aim by hand to keep the link with Earth.
  • Energy & O₂: circuit breakers, life support and a solar field you can see through a window.
  • Hydroponics & kitchen: crop trays, a spirulina bioreactor and a food processor.
  • Crew quarters: a dosimeter and a radiation shelter.
  • Central hub: a tool wall, an electronics repair bench and a spare-parts locker.

Every turn follows one loop: diagnose, then reroute, repair or conserve, then live with the result. Things break on a schedule and in response to what you do:

  • A relay burns out.
  • A dust storm covers the solar panels.
  • A fan fails.
  • The hull starts leaking.
  • A real solar particle storm sends you running to the shelter.

You pick up tools, put two of them in the holsters on your belt, aim them at broken parts and hold the trigger to repair them. Messages to and from Earth arrive after the real light-time delay between the two planets.

Under the hood, a headless simulation runs on fixed ticks and owns all game state: power, oxygen, CO₂, temperature, water, food, spare parts, signal strength and health. The VR layer only sends requests (“intents”) and reacts to the events the simulation sends back, so all the game rules can be tested without a headset.

Benefits and intended impact

  • It teaches real mission-engineering trade-offs. The systems depend on each other, so no single bar can be managed on its own:
    • Turning off the lights saves power, but the crew stops healing.
    • Letting the base get cold slows the crops.
    • Cleaning the solar panels costs battery charge.
    • The storm warning only arrives if you kept the antenna aligned.
  • It uses real NASA and CSA science. The radiation readings, the solar storm of 20 May 2024 recorded by the Curiosity rover’s radiation detector (MSL RAD), Earth–Mars orbital distances and light delay (JPL), dust build-up on panels (Mars Pathfinder), crops studied for life-support systems (quinoa, spirulina), astronaut health studies (NASA OSDR) and live space weather from NASA DONKI all come from real datasets. Every source is credited inside the game.
  • It’s accessible. You can play in Spanish or English. Picture-based panels, “Info” sheets and guided step-by-step tasks make it usable for younger players and non-experts.
  • Intended impact: students and the public come away understanding why surviving on Mars is an engineering problem about limits on energy, air, food, communications and repairs, and they learn it by doing rather than reading.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Area

What we used

Hardware

Meta Quest 3, played in the Quest Browser

Languages

JavaScript (ES modules) with JSDoc type checking, JSON for game data and text

3D and VR

Three.js and WebXR

Build and runtime

Vite, Node 22, npm

Events

mitt event bus between the simulation and the presentation

Testing

Vitest for the headless simulation, plus npm run sim, a balance report that plays automated runs with different strategies

Dev tooling

Meta Immersive Web Emulator and IWER to test VR on a desktop

Data

NASA OSDR (RadLab, MSL RAD, health studies), NASA DONKI, JPL orbital elements, Mars Pathfinder, CSA and NASA NTRS crop data

AI assistance

Claude Code, for help with code and documentation

How it’s creative

  • Real data drives the drama. The solar storm on day 6 replays a real event measured on Mars, and the delay on Earth’s replies is the actual light-travel time.
  • Diegetic interface: almost all information sits on panels, gauges and screens inside the base. The only exception is a small alert banner the team agreed on, which lists faults and the room they’re in.
  • Physical, hands-on repairs: you spin a screwdriver, swing a wrench, use a soldering iron on a circuit board and seal leaks with foam. You can watch a cleaning robot brush the panels outside the window, and drive a Perseverance-style rover from first person to bring back spare parts and rock samples.
  • Science versus survival: rock samples score science points with Earth but don’t keep you alive. Salvaged parts do, so each rover trip forces a choice.

Factors the team considered

  • Comfort and safety in VR: teleport is the default way to move, smooth movement is optional and comes with a vignette, the game pauses automatically when you take the headset off, and there’s no clutter fixed to your view.
  • Performance on a standalone headset: we target 72 Hz with a budget of under 150 draw calls and kept the maximum we measured at 59. That meant merged geometry, instanced plants, baked lighting and no post-processing.
  • Scientific accuracy versus fun: real data sets the rules, but the balance is tuned so that every crisis can be recovered from by sacrificing something else.
  • Two people, two days: we built it at a 14–15 November 2026 hackathon. Each person owned three rooms, shared files only changed through small announced pull requests, and every number and piece of text lives in data files so we could tune without touching code.
  • Language and age: full Spanish and English text, minimum text sizes and contrast levels, and picture-based guidance.
  • Testability: because the simulation runs without graphics, we could test and balance it without a headset.
